title: Red-Cell Indices and the Too-High MCHC
summary: Build MCV, MCH and MCHC from three numbers, watch normal cells turn into hypochromic cells or spherocytes, and catch the cold-agglutinin artifact that fakes a sky-high MCHC.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 31 Hit 1 (core: high MCHC and spherocytosis) with corrections, Hit 4 (index formulas), Trap 3 and the Figure 31 memory anchor. The reviewer’s “increased only in spherocytosis” is corrected: xerocytosis also raises MCHC, and cold agglutinins and other interferences raise it spuriously (see register flag rv-mchc-only).

objectives: Calculate MCV, MCH and MCHC and state what each describes.
Explain why spherocytes and dehydrated cells have a high MCHC, and why a normal MCHC does not exclude spherocytosis.
Recognize a spuriously high MCHC from cold agglutinins and correct it by warming and rerunning.

scenes.title: An MCHC of 41
scenes.altText: An analyzer printout shows MCHC 41 g/dL, flagged high. Two explanation tokens appear: “Spherocytes?” and “Something wrong with the sample?”. A tube sits on a cold bench, beside a snowflake label: the sample has cooled.

cues.text: The analyzer reports an MCHC of 41 grams per decilitre. That is very high.
Is this patient full of spherocytes? Or is something wrong with the sample itself?
To decide, you need to know what MCHC really measures — and how the analyzer calculates it.

props.label: Sample sat on a cold bench

scenes.title: Normal: three indices, three questions
scenes.altText: Three cards build the red-cell indices from a worked example (Hb 15 g/dL, Hct 45%, RBC 5.0 ×10¹²/L). MCV = Hct ÷ RBC: how big is each cell? (45% × 10 ÷ 5.0 = 90 fL). MCH = Hb ÷ RBC: how much hemoglobin per cell? (15 × 10 ÷ 5.0 = 30 pg). MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct: how tightly is hemoglobin packed in the cells? (15 ÷ 45 × 100 = 33 g/dL). A note: on many analyzers the Hct is itself calculated from RBC count × MCV.

cues.text: Start with three measured numbers: hemoglobin 15 grams per decilitre, hematocrit 45 percent, and a red-cell count of 5 million per microlitre.
MCV asks how big each cell is: hematocrit divided by red-cell count. 45 times 10, divided by 5, is 90 femtolitres.
MCH asks how much hemoglobin each cell carries: hemoglobin divided by red-cell count. 15 times 10, divided by 5, is 30 picograms.
MCHC asks how tightly hemoglobin is packed: hemoglobin divided by hematocrit. 15 divided by 45, times 100, is about 33 grams per decilitre.
One detail matters later. Many analyzers don’t measure the hematocrit directly; they calculate it from the red-cell count and MCV.

props.label: Many analyzers calculate Hct = RBC × MCV

scenes.title: What changes: thin, normal and over-packed cells
scenes.altText: Three schematic smear fields. Left: pale hypochromic cells with wide central pallor — low MCHC. Middle: normal cells with central pallor about a third of the diameter. Right: small round spherocytes with no central pallor — the cells have lost membrane and water, so hemoglobin is more concentrated and MCHC rises. A card adds that dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (xerocytosis) also raises MCHC, and that in one study an MCHC above 35.5 g/dL detected only about 41% of hereditary spherocytosis cases.

cues.text: MCHC is a concentration. Low MCHC means cells are thinly filled with hemoglobin: hypochromia, with wide pale centres.
Normal cells have a pale centre about a third of the cell’s width.
Spherocytes have lost membrane and water. They are smaller and rounder, with no pale centre, and their hemoglobin is more concentrated. MCHC goes up.
Spherocytosis is the classic cause, but not the only true one. Dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis, also called xerocytosis, raises MCHC too.
And a high MCHC is a clue, not a test. In one study, an MCHC above 35.5 picked up only about 41 percent of hereditary spherocytosis cases.

props.label: MCHC > 35.5: only ~41% of HS cases detected (one study)

scenes.title: In the lab: when MCHC is too high to be true
scenes.altText: A schematic field shows red cells drifting together into clumps as a thermometer token drops — cold agglutinins. A chain of arrows: clumps counted as fewer cells → RBC count falsely low → calculated Hct falsely low → Hb (measured after lysis) unchanged → MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct falsely high. Then the fix: warm the sample to 37 °C and rerun; the cells separate and MCHC returns to normal. A card notes that labs treat an MCHC of about 37–38.5 g/dL or more as a reason to look for an artifact, and that MCHC is one of the most useful signals that some CBC result is spurious.

cues.text: Now the cold sample. Some patients have cold agglutinins: antibodies that clump red cells when blood cools.
The analyzer counts a clump as one cell, or not at all. The red-cell count falls, so the calculated hematocrit falls too.
Hemoglobin is measured after the cells are lysed, so it barely changes. Hemoglobin divided by a falsely low hematocrit gives a falsely high MCHC.
The fix: warm the sample to 37 degrees and run it again. The clumps break up and the indices come back to normal.
That is why an MCHC above about 37 makes a lab look for an artifact first. MCHC is one of the best alarms that some CBC result is spurious.

props.title: MCHC ≳ 37 g/dL → look for an artifact first
lines: Other causes include high bilirubin; check the sample and the smear

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “MCHC 41 = spherocytosis” is crossed out → “First rule out an artifact (cold agglutinins): warm, rerun, review the smear.” Trap card: “Low MCHC = iron deficiency” is crossed out → “Low MCHC means hypochromia; iron deficiency is one cause, not the only one.”

cues.text: Trap one: an MCHC of 41 does not mean spherocytosis. Values that high are more often an artifact, such as cold agglutinins. Warm the sample, rerun it, and look at the smear.
Trap two: a low MCHC does not prove iron deficiency. It means hypochromia, and iron deficiency is only one cause.
The direction to remember: low MCHC is common; a truly high MCHC is rare and points to spherocytes or dehydrated cells.

props.title: ✗ “MCHC 41 = spherocytosis.”
lines: ✓ Rule out artifact first: warm, rerun, review the smear

props.title: ✗ “Low MCHC = iron deficiency.”
lines: ✓ Low MCHC = hypochromia — iron deficiency is one cause

props.label: Low MCHC: common · truly high MCHC: rare (spherocytes, dehydrated cells)

scenes.title: MCHC is the paint density
scenes.altText: Memory aid: three paint cans. A thin coat (hypochromic, low MCHC), a normal coat, and a thick coat in a small round can (spherocyte, high MCHC). A fourth can overflows past a “37” line, labelled “Too thick to be true → check the sample”. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: MCHC is paint density. Thin paint is hypochromia. Thick paint in a small round can is a spherocyte. Paint so thick it overflows the can — past about 37 — check the sample.
Where it breaks: MCHC is calculated, not seen, so any error in hemoglobin or hematocrit moves it. A normal MCHC doesn’t rule out spherocytosis, and cut-offs depend on the analyzer and the lab.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct: how tightly cells are packed”, “Truly high MCHC: spherocytes or dehydrated cells”, “MCHC ≳ 37: rule out artifact (cold agglutinins) first”.

cues.text: MCHC is hemoglobin divided by hematocrit; a truly high value means spherocytes or dehydrated cells, but a very high one is first a reason to look for an artifact such as cold agglutinins.

props.label: MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct: how tightly cells are packed
Truly high MCHC: spherocytes or dehydrated cells
MCHC ≳ 37: rule out artifact (cold agglutinins) first

explanation.what: Plain language: the indices describe the average red cell — its size, how much hemoglobin it carries, and how tightly that hemoglobin is packed. Scientific terms: MCV = Hct (%) × 10 ÷ RBC (×10¹²/L) in fL; MCH = Hb (g/dL) × 10 ÷ RBC in pg; MCHC = Hb (g/dL) ÷ Hct (%) × 100 in g/dL.
explanation.why: MCHC is a concentration. Hypochromic cells have a low MCHC. Spherocytes lose membrane and become dehydrated through abnormal cation leak, concentrating hemoglobin; dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (xerocytosis) also raises MCHC. Because MCHC is calculated, an error in Hb or Hct moves it: cold agglutinins clump cells, lowering the RBC count and calculated Hct while Hb (measured after lysis) is unchanged, so MCHC rises falsely.
explanation.measure: Analyzers measure Hb and RBC count (and MCV) and derive the others; many calculate Hct = RBC × MCV. An MCHC above about 37–38.5 g/dL is used as a trigger to look for artifacts; warming the sample (37 °C for about 2 h, or short heating at 41 °C) and rerunning corrects cold-agglutinin effects. High bilirubin can also falsely raise MCHC.
explanation.differs: True high MCHC (spherocytes, xerocytosis) vs spurious high MCHC (cold agglutinins, interference); low MCHC (hypochromia from any cause) vs iron deficiency specifically.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: index calculations, which index rises in spherocytosis, recognition of a cold-agglutinin pattern (low RBC, high MCV and MCHC) and its fix (warm to 37 °C and rerun), and the trap that low MCHC is not specific to iron deficiency.

mnemonic.text: MCHC is paint density — overflow past 37 means check the sample.
mnemonic.explanation: Thin paint is hypochromia, thick paint in a small round can is a spherocyte, and paint so thick it overflows the can (above about 37 g/dL) usually means a measurement artifact.
mnemonic.limitation: MCHC is calculated, so any Hb or Hct error moves it; a normal MCHC does not exclude spherocytosis; artifact cut-offs (about 37–38.5 g/dL) depend on the analyzer and laboratory.

analogyLimitations: Paint cans are a memory device; hemoglobin is not a surface coat.
Smear fields and clumps are schematic, not real morphology.
The CBC values in the example are invented.
takeaway: MCHC is hemoglobin divided by hematocrit; a truly high value means spherocytes or dehydrated cells, but a very high one is first a reason to look for an artifact such as cold agglutinins.

questions.stem: Hb 12 g/dL, Hct 36%, RBC 4.0 ×10¹²/L. What are the MCV and MCHC?

options.rationale: Incorrect. 30 is the MCH (12 × 10 ÷ 4.0 = 30 pg), not the MCV.
Incorrect. MCHC uses Hct in percent: 12 ÷ 36 × 100 ≈ 33.
Incorrect. The factor of 10 (MCV) and 100 (MCHC) were left out.

questions.stem: A sample left on a cold bench gives RBC 2.1 ×10¹²/L, MCV 118 fL and MCHC 42 g/dL, with grainy clumps on the smear. What is the best next step?

options.text: Warm the sample to 37 °C and rerun
options.rationale: Correct. This pattern suggests cold agglutinins; warming disperses the clumps and corrects the RBC count and indices.
Incorrect. An MCHC this high with clumps points to an artifact; spherocytosis is not diagnosed from MCHC alone.
Incorrect. The high MCV and low RBC count are likely caused by clumps counted as large cells or not counted at all.
Incorrect. Cooling makes cold agglutination worse.

questions.stem: Why is the MCHC raised in hereditary spherocytosis?

options.text: The cells lose membrane and water, concentrating their hemoglobin
options.rationale: Correct. Membrane loss and cation leak dehydrate the cells, so hemoglobin per volume rises.

options.text: The cells contain more hemoglobin molecules than normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hemoglobin per cell (MCH) is not increased; the cell volume falls.

options.text: Spherocytes are larger than normal cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Spherocytes are smaller and denser, not larger.
Incorrect. Iron stores do not change the hemoglobin concentration inside a cell.

claims.text: Spherocytes (dehydration from cation leak) and xerocytosis raise MCHC.
MCHC > 35.5 g/dL detected about 41% of HS cases (specificity ~94%) in one study; raised bilirubin can falsely increase MCHC.
Cold agglutinins lower the RBC count and falsely raise MCHC; warming (37 °C ~2 h, or 41 °C briefly) and rerunning corrects it; labs use MCHC ≥ 370–385 g/L as a trigger.
An error in one measured parameter alters calculated indices; MCHC is a key alarm for spurious results.
MCV = Hct (%) × 10 ÷ RBC; MCH = Hb × 10 ÷ RBC; MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct (%) × 100.
claims.note: The formulas follow from the definitions (units check: 0.45 L/L ÷ 5.0 × 10¹²/L = 90 fL), but no external reference stating them was read; NCBI Bookshelf was blocked.

claims.text: Many analyzers calculate Hct from RBC × MCV, and Hb is measured after lysis so clumping barely changes it.
claims.note: Mechanism consistent with the sources read but not stated in them.

claims.text: Low MCHC means hypochromia, of which iron deficiency is one cause.
claims.note: Other causes (e.g. thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia) were not checked for this lesson.

claims.text: Paint cans, smear fields and clumps.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says MCHC is increased only in spherocytosis; xerocytosis also raises it and several artifacts raise it spuriously. The lesson teaches the corrected statement.

morphology.note: Smear fields, spherocytes and clumps are schematic drawings, not real morphology; review real smears for spherocytes and agglutination.
